continuity_scope: C. S. Lewis, The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe: A Story for Children (London: Geoffrey Bles, 1950), the first Narnia novel published. This is a single-novel, original-English, publication-order witness, not a composite series account. Exact chapter locators are used because pagination varies among impressions and editions.

coverage_rule: Include the four named Pevensie siblings, the named faun who first receives Lucy, the named Beaver guide, Aslan, and the individual designated in this novel as the White Witch. This compact eight-person cohort covers the portal entry, betrayal pressure, guidance, and central conflict. Named but briefer figures (Professor Kirke, Father Christmas, the Dwarf, Fenris Ulf, Maugrim, and others), unnamed speakers, collectives, creatures as kinds, places, artifacts, and narrative/cosmological concepts remain outside the character graph.
omissions: The other six Narnia novels, whether arranged by publication or internal chronology; their later names, explanations, events, and outcomes are not imported
All stage, radio, television, film, game, and other adaptations; adaptation-only casting, plot, visual design, and dialogue
Translations, retellings, abridgments, audiobook performances, and illustrations as independent continuity evidence
Named minor figures and collective peoples/species, as well as Narnia, the wardrobe, the Stone Table, prophecy, law, theology, and allegorical readings as character nodes
uncertainties: The title has appeared in different series sequences. This pass follows the documented 1950 publication witness only; it does not adjudicate preferred reading order or treat later internal chronology as evidence.
First-edition and later printing pagination differ. Chapter titles 1–17 are the stable primary-text locators; no later-edition page number is presented as if it were a 1950 page.
The individual is called the White Witch in this novel. Later-series names or biography are excluded, rather than retroactively attaching them to this witness.

The novel has often received Christian or allegorical interpretation. Records describe fictional text-level actions and terms only; they neither assert theological equivalence nor map fictional characters to religious figures, peoples, or real cultures.
The work remains copyright-controlled in many jurisdictions. Evidence records use bibliographic/authorized viewing sources and chapter locators, with no extended quotation.
evidence_basis: Primary-text claims are anchored to named chapters in the declared 1950 English novel; Google Books' bibliographic/viewer record supports limited text-location cross-checking. The Open British National Bibliography and British Library supply institutional publication metadata. No fan wiki or Wikipedia is used.
